concepts.title: Bar Magnet and Its Field Lines
concepts.definition: Iron filings around a magnet trace curves that always run north to south outside and close through the magnet itself; the tangent at any point gives the local field direction, and two such curves can never meet.
concepts.formula: field_direction = tangent of field line at each point
concepts.key_idea: Because isolated poles cannot be cut off a magnet, every field-line loop is closed; denser lines mean a stronger field.
question_patterns: why do magnetic field lines always close on themselves
can two field lines cross each other in a magnetic field
what does the tangent to a field line tell you about the field there
a bar magnet is sliced in half; what happens to its poles
how do the field patterns of a magnet and a current-carrying solenoid compare
where around a bar magnet is the field strongest according to the line density

solution_steps.explain: lines leave the north face, swing around outside, and re-enter the south face with no start or end
tangent gives B direction; crowding of lines gives B magnitude
an intersection would give two field directions at once, which is impossible

concepts.title: Solenoid Picture of a Bar Magnet
concepts.definition: A magnetised bar behaves like a tightly wound coil of circulating currents: slicing it yields two weaker magnets just as cutting a solenoid yields two shorter ones, and its moment equals that of the matching coil.
concepts.key_idea: Far along the axis, solenoid and bar magnet produce the same 1 over distance cubed field, so the two are interchangeable as dipoles.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph105.txt section 5.2.2 (Eq. 5.1, finite solenoid axial field, Example 5.1)
question_patterns: explain why a bar magnet can be treated as a solenoid with circulating currents
what do you get when a magnet is broken across its middle
compare the far axial field of a finite solenoid with that of a magnet
an iron nail near a magnet feels a pull but a needle in a uniform field does not; why
how would you decide which of two identical bars is the magnetised one using only the bars
does every magnetic setup need a distinct north and south face

solution_steps.action: replace the magnet by circulating currents
solution_steps.explain: each current loop adds a dipole moment pointing the same way
halving the bar halves the coil, giving two weaker dipoles with fresh pole pairs
the 1 over distance cubed axial decay agrees for coil and bar, fixing the equivalent moment

concepts.title: Torque on a Magnetic Dipole
concepts.definition: A compass needle free to swing in a uniform field feels a restoring twist of size mB sin(theta) that tries to line its moment up with the field; uniformity removes any net push, leaving pure rotation.
concepts.key_idea: The twist vanishes when the needle sits along the field and peaks at right angles, which is how a suspended magnet settles north-south.
question_patterns: a short bar magnet sits at 30 degrees to a 0.25 T field with torque 4.5e-2 J; find its moment
compute the twist on a magnet of moment m in a uniform field at angle theta
why does a magnet in a uniform field rotate but not translate
find mB sin(theta) for the given needle and field values
what orientation of a suspended magnet gives zero and maximum torque
a solenoid hangs with its axis at an angle to a horizontal field; what torque acts on it

solution_steps.explain: the scale of the interaction is the product mB
the twist magnitude is mB sin(theta)

concepts.title: Potential Energy of a Tilted Dipole
concepts.definition: Turning a needle away from the field stores energy; with the zero chosen at right angles, the energy at tilt theta reads minus mB cos(theta), lowest when aligned and highest when flipped.
concepts.key_idea: Alignment is the energy minimum at -mB, the flipped state the maximum at +mB, so the needle spontaneously settles along the field.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph105.txt section 5.2.3 (Eq. 5.3, energy minimum and maximum, Exercise 5.2)
question_patterns: write the potential energy of a magnetic dipole at angle theta to the field
a 0.32 J/T magnet in a 0.15 T field sits stable and then flipped; give both energies
why is the aligned position of a magnet the most stable one
evaluate minus mB cos(theta) for a needle at right angles to the field
where is the zero of dipole potential energy usually placed
compare the energy of a magnet pointing with and against the applied field

solution_steps.explain: energy swings between plus and minus this product

solution_steps.action: apply the cosine of the tilt
solution_steps.explain: U = -mB cos(theta) with zero at 90 degrees

concepts.title: Work to Rotate a Magnet in a Field
concepts.definition: An external agent swinging a magnet between two tilts must supply the change in dipole energy, mB times the cosine gap between the start and finish angles.
concepts.key_idea: Swinging from aligned to perpendicular costs mB; carrying on to antiparallel doubles the bill to 2mB.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph105.txt section 5.2.3 (energy integration, Exercise 5.5 work parts)
question_patterns: how much work turns a magnet from along the field to across it
compute the energy needed to flip a magnet to point against the field
a 1.5 J/T magnet aligned in a 0.22 T field is turned normal; find the work done
what external work moves a dipole from tilt one to tilt two
find mB times the cosine difference for a rotation in a uniform field
is the torque nonzero after the magnet is held normal to the field

solution_steps.explain: U1 = -mB cos(theta1)
U2 = -mB cos(theta2)
the applied work equals U2 minus U1

concepts.title: Axial Field of a Short Bar Magnet
concepts.definition: On the magnet's axis, far compared with its length, the field is twice the dipole benchmark: mu0 times 2m over 4 pi r cubed, pointing along the moment.
concepts.key_idea: The axial point gets double weight because the two pole contributions add along the axis instead of partly cancelling.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph105.txt section 5.2.4 (Eq. 5.5, Table 5.1 axial row, Example 5.7 data)
question_patterns: a 0.48 J/T magnet sits 10 cm away on its axis; find the field there
compute mu0 2m over 4 pi r cubed for a short magnet
what field does a bar magnet produce at a point on its axis far away
compare the axial and equatorial field strengths of the same magnet
determine the on-axis field at a stated distance from a magnet's centre
how does the axial field fall when the distance from the magnet doubles

solution_steps.explain: the base cube-law term is mu0 m over 4 pi r cubed
B axial equals 2 times the base term

concepts.title: Equatorial Field of a Short Bar Magnet
concepts.definition: On the magnet's perpendicular bisector, again far out, the field is the single dipole benchmark mu0 m over 4 pi r cubed, aimed opposite the moment direction.
concepts.key_idea: Equator to axis strength runs 1 to 2 for the same distance, mirroring the electric dipole pattern with mu0 standing in for 1 over epsilon0.
question_patterns: find the field of a 0.48 J/T magnet on its normal bisector 10 cm out
compute mu0 m over 4 pi r cubed at an equatorial point
what is the field on the perpendicular bisector of a short magnet
why does the equatorial field point opposite to the magnetic moment
how many times weaker is the equatorial field than the axial one at equal distance
determine the sideways field of a bar magnet at a far-off bisector point

solution_steps.explain: the equatorial result is exactly mu0 m over 4 pi r cubed

concepts.title: Gauss Law for Magnetic Fields
concepts.definition: Wrap any closed surface around magnets, coils or empty space: the outward and inward field-line counts always balance, so the total magnetic flux through the surface adds to zero because no isolated pole exists.
concepts.key_idea: Zero net flux is the magnetic twin of Gauss's electric law with the charge side missing, and a hypothetical monopole would restore a mu0 qm right side.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph105.txt section 5.3 (Eq. 5.6, Example 5.3-5.4 flux and monopole discussion)
question_patterns: state the flux rule that holds for every closed surface in magnetism
why is the total B-flux through a closed box around a magnet zero
how would the magnetic flux law change if monopoles were discovered
which of the drawn field-line pictures violate the flux rule
compare Gauss's law for magnetic and electric fields
do field lines emanating from a single point describe a possible magnetic field

solution_steps.explain: each patch carries a flux B dot dS in or out
every entering line must leave somewhere, so contributions cancel
the sum over all patches vanishes for any closed surface because dipole lines never terminate

concepts.title: Magnetisation of a Sample
concepts.definition: A material's magnetisation is its net dipole moment squeezed into each unit volume, quoted in A/m; atomic loop moments add vectorially to build it.
concepts.key_idea: M measures how strongly a chunk of matter is magnetised per unit volume, independent of how big the chunk is.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph105.txt section 5.4 (Eq. 5.7, dimensions L-1 A, units A m-1)
question_patterns: define the magnetisation vector of a material sample
compute moment per unit volume for a specimen of known net moment
what are the units of magnetisation and how is it built from atomic moments
a core carries net moment in a given volume; find M
how does magnetisation differ from the total magnetic moment
find the A/m value of M for a small magnetised rod

solution_steps.explain: M is defined as net dipole moment over sample volume

concepts.title: Magnetisation M and Intensity H
concepts.definition: The intensity H keeps track of only the free driving current (n times I inside a solenoid), while M records the material's own response; together they rebuild the total field as B = mu0 (H + M).
concepts.key_idea: H is material-blind: the same solenoid current gives the same H whether the core is empty, glass or iron.
question_patterns: compute H inside a solenoid of 1000 turns per metre carrying 2 A
what does the magnetic intensity H depend on and what does it ignore
relate B, H and M for material inside a current-carrying coil
find nI for the given winding density and current
why is H independent of the core filling the solenoid
a wound core carries current I; obtain the intensity inside it

solution_steps.explain: for a solenoid the intensity is simply H = nI

concepts.title: Field Inside a Material Core
concepts.definition: Filling a solenoid with matter of relative permeability mur multiplies the vacuum field: B = mu0 mur H, so a mur of 400 boosts the interior field four-hundredfold over the empty coil.
concepts.key_idea: The material's aligned moments add their own field Bm = mu0 M on top of the driving field, which is how iron cores strengthen electromagnets.
question_patterns: a solenoid with 1000 turns per metre and 2 A has a core of relative permeability 400; find B
compute the interior field when a magnetic core fills a current-carrying coil
how much does a high-permeability core raise the solenoid field
evaluate mu0 mur H for the given core and winding data
find the extra field contributed by a magnetised core over the vacuum value
work out the magnetising current that would replace an iron core

solution_steps.explain: H = nI comes from the free current alone
B = mu0 mur H multiplies the vacuum response by mur

concepts.title: Susceptibility and Permeability Relations
concepts.definition: For a linear material the response is proportional to the drive, M = chi H, and the bookkeeping closes with mur = 1 + chi and mu = mu0 mur, so one number fixes all three.
concepts.key_idea: Susceptibility chi is the dial that separates material classes: slightly negative for diamagnets, slightly positive for paramagnets, huge for ferromagnets.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph105.txt section 5.4 (Eqs. 5.13-5.15, Table 5.2 chi and mur ranges)
question_patterns: how are susceptibility, relative permeability and permeability linked
given chi find mur and mu for a material
what sign and size of chi marks a diamagnet, paramagnet and ferromagnet
compute mur = 1 + chi for a stated susceptibility
why is only one of chi, mur and mu independent
relate M to H for a linear magnetic material

solution_steps.explain: M = chi H says the material's moment density follows the drive linearly
relative permeability is mur = 1 + chi
the absolute permeability mu = mu0 mur carries the same units as mu0

concepts.title: Diamagnetic Behaviour
concepts.definition: Materials whose atoms carry no net moment develop an induced moment opposing an applied field, so they drift toward weaker field regions and are gently pushed away from a magnet; chi is small and negative.
concepts.formula: chi less than 0 with mur less than 1
concepts.key_idea: Lenz-law induced currents inside atoms explain the repulsion; superconductors are the extreme case with chi = -1, expelling field completely (Meissner effect).
question_patterns: why is a diamagnetic bar repelled by a magnet rather than attracted
what happens to field lines entering a diamagnetic sample
name a few diamagnetic materials and their susceptibility range
how do orbiting electrons explain diamagnetism
what makes a superconductor a perfect diamagnet
a diamagnetic rod rests in a non-uniform field; which way does it drift

solution_steps.explain: the applied field slows electrons orbiting one way and speeds the others, a Lenz-law effect leaving an opposing net moment
field lines partially avoid the sample, lowering B inside by about one part in 1e5
negative susceptibility places the substance in the diamagnetic class; -1 marks the perfect case

concepts.title: Paramagnetic Behaviour
concepts.definition: Atoms with permanent moments line up only feebly with an applied field because heat keeps scrambling them, so these substances are weakly pulled toward strong field regions; chi is small and positive.
concepts.formula: chi greater than 0 with mur slightly above 1
concepts.key_idea: Cooling or strengthening the field increases alignment until saturation, where every atomic moment points along the field.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph105.txt section 5.5.2 (paramagnetic list, temperature dependence, Fig. 5.7b)
question_patterns: why does a paramagnetic rod move into the stronger part of a field
how do temperature and field strength control paramagnetic alignment
name some paramagnetic substances
what is saturation magnetisation in a paramagnet
compare the field inside a paramagnet with the applied field
how do thermal motions prevent full alignment of atomic moments

solution_steps.explain: each atom owns a permanent dipole moment even before any field arrives
the field tips moments toward itself while thermal motion resists, giving a slight interior field boost
lower temperature or stronger field raises M until every moment points along B

concepts.title: Ferromagnetism and Domains
concepts.definition: In iron-group substances, neighbouring atomic moments lock into meter-scale-swaths called domains that snap into common alignment under even tiny fields, giving susceptibilities in the thousands and a strong pull toward magnets.
concepts.formula: chi much greater than 1 with mur much greater than 1
concepts.key_idea: Hard ferromagnets keep their magnetisation after the field leaves (permanent magnets); soft ones lose it; strong heating destroys domains and turns the sample paramagnetic.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph105.txt section 5.5.3 (domains, hard vs soft materials, temperature loss)
question_patterns: what are domains and how do they explain strong magnetisation
why does soft iron lose its magnetisation while alnico keeps it
what happens to a ferromagnet heated well above its transition temperature
how do field lines behave around and inside a ferromagnetic sample
distinguish hard and soft ferromagnetic materials with examples
why is the relative permeability of iron above one thousand

solution_steps.explain: quantum coupling aligns millions of atomic moments inside each domain even with no external field
an applied field enlarges favourably oriented domains and rotates the rest, concentrating field lines strongly
removing the field leaves hard materials magnetised and soft ones demagnetised; high temperature collapses the domain order
